design_detail: Retrospective chart-review cohort of 376 consecutive patients admitted with chest pain and a urine toxicology screen positive for cocaine at the two major hospitals affiliated with an academic teaching university (Saint Louis University), January 2000 to December 2007. Patients were identified by a positive immunoassay urine drug screen plus reported cocaine use within the previous 24 hours, then by ICD-9 codes for chest pain, angina or chest discomfort, with every chart reviewed manually by physician members of the research team to exclude chest pain diagnosed as pulmonary in the emergency department. The exposure is whether a beta blocker was given in the first 24 hours of presentation (164 patients, 44%) against not (212). The outcome is a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or all-cause death during the index hospitalization. Because the two groups differed substantially at baseline, the authors built a propensity score for receiving a beta blocker from 13 pre-treatment characteristics, stratified the cohort by propensity-score quintile and fitted a logistic regression adjusted for that quintile.
can_establish: How often beta blockers were actually given to patients with cocaine-positive chest pain at two urban hospitals over eight years despite guidance against it, which drugs were used, and whether in-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia and death were more common in those who received one, with the imprecision that about 52 events across 376 patients allows.
cannot_establish: Whether beta blockers are safe in this setting: the adjusted interval runs from a 36% reduction to a near-tripling of the composite outcome, so the study excludes neither substantial harm nor substantial benefit. It also cannot establish that the patients had pharmacologically active cocaine on board when the drug was given (a urine screen stays positive for days), that the two groups were comparable after adjustment (the treated group received far more of every other anti-ischemic therapy, none of it in the propensity model), or that the timing of the beta blocker relative to the outcome was accounted for.

sample.recruitment: Consecutive patients presenting to two academic hospitals from January 2000 to December 2007 with a urine screen positive for cocaine and reported use within the previous 24 hours, with an ICD-9 code for chest pain, angina or chest discomfort; charts reviewed by hand to exclude pulmonary causes of chest pain diagnosed in the emergency department (p. 1802).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: positive immunoassay urine drug test for cocaine, reported cocaine use within 24 hours, ICD-9 chest-pain code. Excluded: chest pain diagnosed as pulmonary in the emergency department (for example pneumonia or pulmonary embolus) (p. 1802). No exclusion for critical illness, and no restriction by age.
sample.demographics: Beta-blocker group against no beta blocker: mean age 46 +/- 9 against 42 +/- 11 years (p < 0.001); 32% against 26% women; 10% against 13% recorded as White and 81% against 76% as Black; chest pain typical for angina 17% against 8% (p = 0.012); history of hypertension 80% against 38%, hyperlipidemia 23% against 11%, diabetes 25% against 14%, known coronary artery disease 33% against 13% (all p <= 0.005); TIMI risk score 0 in 44% against 69% (p < 0.001); systolic pressure 152 +/- 36 against 138 +/- 32 mm Hg and diastolic 89 +/- 26 against 80 +/- 22 mm Hg (both p < 0.001); heart rate 91 +/- 22 against 94 +/- 25 beats/min (p = 0.29) (Table 1, p. 1803).
sample.attrition: Not applicable: a complete-admission chart review with in-hospital outcomes. No patient is reported excluded for missing data, and how missing chart items were handled is not described.
sample.selection_effects: Two urban academic hospitals with a predominantly Black patient population, over a period when guidelines already advised against beta blockers here, so the 44% who received one were selected by their clinicians precisely on grounds related to the outcome: they were older, had more coronary risk factors and known coronary disease, higher TIMI scores, higher presenting blood pressure and worse left ventricular function, and they were far more often admitted to a cardiac intensive care unit (22% against 8%). Treatment is therefore confounded by indication in both directions at once, since the sicker patients also received more of every protective therapy.

exposure.measurement: Beta-blocker administration within the first 24 hours of presentation, taken from the hospital chart along with all other cardiac medications given in that window (p. 1802). Cocaine exposure established by immunoassay urine drug test (Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics) plus reported use within the previous 24 hours; no quantitative cocaine or metabolite measurement, no route and no amount (p. 1802).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Doses, routes and timing of the beta blockers are not reported, only the agent: metoprolol in 74 patients, labetalol in 44, carvedilol in 43 and atenolol in 3 (p. 1803). Of the 164, 77 received a beta-1 selective drug and 87 received carvedilol or labetalol, which the paper groups as nonselective although both also block alpha receptors (editors' arithmetic from the same sentence).
exposure.polysubstance: Not characterized. No alcohol or other drug use is reported, although cocaine and alcohol are commonly used together and cocaethylene affects the heart. Co-prescribed cardiac drugs differed sharply between groups and are reported: aspirin 84% against 57%, clopidogrel 23% against 8%, systemic anticoagulation 23% against 9%, nitrates 50% against 36%, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors 72% against 24% (all p <= 0.007; Table 1, p. 1803). None of these co-treatments was included in the propensity score.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Unknown and acknowledged as a limitation: a urine screen can stay positive for 48 to 72 hours after use, so how recently cocaine had been taken, and whether it was still pharmacologically active when the beta blocker was given, cannot be established (p. 1805).

comparison.controls: The 212 patients with cocaine-positive chest pain at the same two hospitals in the same period who were not given a beta blocker in the first 24 hours.
comparison.matching: No matching despite the table heading. The analysis stratified patients into propensity-score quintiles and fitted a logistic regression adjusted for quintile; the propensity score was built from age, gender, race, character of chest pain, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, known HIV infection, previous lung disease, previous coronary artery disease, TIMI risk score, blood pressures, and initial electrocardiographic findings and cardiac biomarkers, with a C statistic of 0.82 (pp. 1802, 1804).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The amount, route and timing of cocaine use; alcohol and other drug use; the co-prescribed cardiac drugs that differed greatly between groups; the clinical reasoning that led a physician to give or withhold the drug in each case; and the timing of the beta blocker relative to the event counted as the outcome.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: All patients in both groups were cocaine-positive by urine screen; the comparison is between treatment decisions, not between cocaine exposure and none.

outcomes.instruments: Hospital records: death, myocardial infarction, stroke and ventricular arrhythmia during the chest-pain admission, with electrocardiograms, telemetry strips, troponin T and creatine kinase-MB, echocardiography and stress tests as clinically obtained (p. 1802).
outcomes.validity_norms: Myocardial infarction was defined as a troponin-T level above the local upper limit of normal or significant ST-segment elevation in two contiguous leads with chest pain or an anginal equivalent; stroke and ventricular arrhythmias were identified clinically by the treating physicians, not by an independent or blinded adjudicator (p. 1803). Clinical identification by treating physicians who knew what had been given is the main outcome-measurement weakness.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Adverse outcome' is the composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or all-cause death during the index hospitalization, with the four components also reported separately (p. 1803, Table 3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 10 counts the composite and its four components, each tested unadjusted and after propensity-score adjustment; the paper also reports two further adjusted comparisons for drug subtypes and about 40 baseline comparisons in Tables 1 and 2, all at p <= 0.05 uncorrected.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. Charts were reviewed by physician members of the research team, and outcomes were those recorded by treating physicians; no blinding of reviewers to beta-blocker status is described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unadjusted rates (Table 3, p. 1804), beta blocker against none: composite end point 16% against 12%, p = 0.32 (the abstract gives 15.9% against 12.3%); death 3% against 6%, p = 0.13; stroke 3% against 3%, p = 1.00; myocardial infarction 5% against 2%, p = 0.18; arrhythmia 7% against 5%, p = 0.52. Editors' calculation from these percentages and the group sizes: roughly 26 composite events in each arm, about 52 in all. Adjusted for propensity-score quintile (Table 3): composite odds ratio 1.37 (95% CI 0.64 to 2.93), p = 0.42; death 0.66 (0.14 to 3.04); stroke 1.20 (0.27 to 5.36); myocardial infarction 1.67 (0.44 to 6.35); arrhythmia 1.24 (0.38 to 3.98). Secondary analysis by drug type (p. 1804): beta-1 selective 1.83 (0.79 to 4.24) and the drugs labelled nonselective 0.90 (0.33 to 2.42), each against no beta blocker; no test of interaction between the two is reported. Cardiac biomarkers were lower in the beta-blocker group (creatine kinase-MB at presentation 3.2 ng/ml, interquartile range 1.8 to 5.5, against 4.5, 2.5 to 10.5, p = 0.006; peak 3.2, 1.7 to 7.1, against 4.9, 2.7 to 12.2, p < 0.001) while troponin T did not differ (peak 0.04 ng/ml, 0.01 to 0.12, against 0.04, 0.01 to 0.21, p = 0.14), and left ventricular ejection fraction was lower in the beta-blocker group (0.41 +/- 0.17 against 0.49 +/- 0.17, p = 0.006) (Table 2, p. 1804).
analysis.covariates: Thirteen pre-treatment characteristics entered the propensity score (listed under comparison > matching); the outcome model adjusted only for propensity-score quintile. Co-prescribed aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation, nitrates and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, which differed by 14 to 48 percentage points between the groups, were not adjusted for at any stage, nor was the timing of the beta blocker relative to the outcome.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration; the study protocol was reviewed and approved by the university's institutional review board (p. 1803).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four components of the composite are reported with both unadjusted rates and adjusted odds ratios, which is complete. The weakness is that the subgroup result pointing in opposite directions for the two drug classes is reported as uniformly null, with no interaction test and no comment on the fact that more than half the beta-blocker group received a drug with alpha-blocking activity, which is the pharmacological crux of the question.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With about 26 events per arm the adjusted confidence interval for the composite spans 0.64 to 2.93, so the data are equally compatible with a one-third reduction and with a near-tripling of risk; the individual components, with 3% to 7% event rates, have intervals up to 0.14 to 3.04. The authors call for a prospective trial (p. 1805).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 376 patients admitted with cocaine-positive chest pain, 44% were given a beta blocker in the first 24 hours even though guidelines advised against it. Those given one were older and sicker on every measured axis and also received far more aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation, nitrates and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. In-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia and death were statistically indistinguishable between the groups, before and after adjustment for a propensity-score quintile, with confidence intervals wide enough to contain both appreciable harm and appreciable benefit.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that no differences in outcomes were observed between patients treated and not treated with beta-blocker therapy, and the discussion goes further: beta-blocker use in these at-risk patients 'may be safe', the therapy was 'at least neutral' and 'could even potentially have had a protective effect', and treatment 'may be safer than previously suggested' (pp. 1802, 1805). The gap is the standard one between a non-significant result and evidence of safety. The adjusted point estimate for the composite is 1.37, that is in the direction of harm, with an upper limit near 3; the point estimate for myocardial infarction is 1.67. A study with about 52 events cannot support a safety claim from these numbers. The authors' argument that the treated group was sicker and did no worse is reasonable as far as it goes, but it is weakened by their having also received much more of every other anti-ischemic therapy, which is never adjusted for. The authors do state the key limitations themselves (retrospective design, chart-documentation quality, residual confounding, inability to date the cocaine use) and they explicitly call for a prospective trial.

timeline.event: Mechanistic origin of the concern: intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow in cocaine-naive catheterization patients
American Heart Association scientific statement advises against beta blockers in the acute setting of cocaine-associated chest pain
This study: no detectable difference in in-hospital outcomes in 376 patients, with wide intervals
Meta-analysis pooling observational studies of this question, including this cohort

replication.where_it_stands: Several retrospective hospital cohorts, this one among them, have failed to detect the harm the mechanistic studies predict, and the authors of each note the same limits: non-random treatment, uncertain timing of cocaine use and too few events. No randomized trial has been done, so the question remains one where mechanism and observational practice data point in different directions without either being decisive.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article carries no funding statement (p. 1806).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state they have no conflicts of interest to disclose (p. 1806).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Division of Cardiology, Christiana Care Health System (Newark, Delaware); Saint Luke's Mid America Heart and Vascular Institute (Kansas City, Missouri); and the Center for Comprehensive Cardiovascular Care, Saint Louis University.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people presenting with chest pain after recent cocaine use, allocating an intravenous beta blocker against the currently recommended alternatives, with a confirmed recent-use measure rather than a urine screen, blinded outcome adjudication, and enough events to exclude a clinically meaningful difference in infarction and arrhythmia. Short of that, a cohort analysis that handles the timing of treatment relative to the event and adjusts for co-prescribed anti-ischemic drugs would at least remove the two largest sources of bias in the existing observational evidence.

domains.note: Treatment was chosen by clinicians on grounds strongly related to the outcome, and the two groups differ on almost every measured characteristic. The propensity score covers 13 baseline variables but none of the co-treatments, which differ by up to 48 percentage points (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors 72% against 24%, aspirin 84% against 57%), nor the amount, route or timing of cocaine use. Confounding here runs in both directions, so its net size and sign are unknown.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Exposure is defined over the first 24 hours while the outcome is counted over the whole admission, so a patient who dies or has an event early is less likely to have been given a beta blocker. No landmark or time-varying analysis addresses this, and the direction of the resulting bias favours the treated group.

Whether a beta blocker was given is recorded in the chart and is unlikely to be misclassified, but dose, route and timing within the 24 hours are not reported, and 87 of the 164 received carvedilol or labetalol, drugs with alpha-blocking activity that the paper classifies simply as nonselective, which blurs the exposure the mechanistic concern is about.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: This is routine care, so the question is co-intervention rather than protocol deviation; the large differences in aspirin, clopidogrel, anticoagulation, nitrates and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are co-interventions that could offset any harm from the beta blocker and are not adjusted for.

Charts were reviewed by hand, which the authors offer as mitigation, but no account is given of missing values in the covariates or outcomes, and echocardiography and stress tests were obtained in only some patients and more often in the treated group.

Death and troponin are hard measures, but stroke and ventricular arrhythmia were identified clinically by treating physicians who knew what had been given, with no blinded adjudication, and one of the paper's own definitions ties myocardial infarction 'associated with beta-blocker use' to changes after administration while the composite counts any in-hospital infarction.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The composite and all four components are reported both ways, which is good practice, but the adjusted odds ratio appears as 1.34 in the Results text and 1.37 in the abstract and Table 3, and the drug-subtype analysis is summarised as uniformly null although its two estimates point in opposite directions and no interaction was tested.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is routine-care data on a question no one has randomized, and it is reported more fully than most such studies, with every component of the composite shown. But treatment was chosen on exactly the grounds that predict the outcome, the exposure window and the outcome window overlap in a way that favours the treated group, the co-treatments that differ most are never adjusted for, and about 52 events cannot support a conclusion of safety. The source can be cited for how often beta blockers were given to patients with cocaine-positive chest pain at two US hospitals in 2000 to 2007, which agents were used, and that in-hospital events were not detectably more common in the treated group, with the adjusted interval 0.64 to 2.93 stated alongside. It cannot be cited for the safety of beta blockers after cocaine use, nor as a refutation of the mechanistic studies, which concern a drug given while cocaine is pharmacologically active, a condition this cohort could not verify.

key_findings.finding: Of 376 consecutive patients admitted with chest pain and a urine screen positive for cocaine at two academic hospitals between January 2000 and December 2007, 164 (44%) received a beta blocker within the first 24 hours, despite guidelines advising against it: metoprolol in 74, labetalol in 44, carvedilol in 43 and atenolol in 3.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic from the same sentence: 77 received a beta-1 selective drug and 87 received carvedilol or labetalol, both of which also block alpha receptors, so more than half the treated group did not receive unopposed beta-blockade.

key_findings.finding: The patients given a beta blocker were older (46 +/- 9 against 42 +/- 11 years) and had more hypertension (80% against 38%), hyperlipidemia (23% against 11%), diabetes (25% against 14%), known coronary artery disease (33% against 13%), typical anginal pain (17% against 8%) and higher TIMI risk scores (all p <= 0.012).

The beta-blocker group also received far more of every other cardiac therapy: aspirin 84% against 57%, clopidogrel 23% against 8%, systemic anticoagulation 23% against 9%, nitrates 50% against 36%, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors 72% against 24% (all p <= 0.007), and were more often admitted to a cardiac intensive care unit (22% against 8%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, other medications ordered and disposition
key_findings.note: None of these co-treatments entered the propensity score, which was built from baseline characteristics only.

key_findings.finding: The composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or death occurred in 16% of the beta-blocker group and 12% of the others (p = 0.32); adjusted for propensity-score quintile the odds ratio was 1.37 (95% CI 0.64 to 2.93), p = 0.42.
key_findings.note: The Results text reports this adjusted odds ratio as 1.34 with the same interval and p value; the abstract and Table 3 give 1.37. Editors' calculation from the percentages: roughly 26 events in each arm.

key_findings.finding: No individual component differed: death 3% against 6% (adjusted odds ratio 0.66, 0.14 to 3.04), stroke 3% against 3% (1.20, 0.27 to 5.36), myocardial infarction 5% against 2% (1.67, 0.44 to 6.35), ventricular arrhythmia 7% against 5% (1.24, 0.38 to 3.98).
key_findings.locator: Table 3, death, stroke, MI and arrhythmia rows
key_findings.note: Every interval is wide enough to include both appreciable harm and appreciable benefit.

key_findings.finding: In the secondary analysis by drug class, the adjusted odds ratio against no beta blocker was 1.83 (0.79 to 4.24) for beta-1 selective drugs and 0.90 (0.33 to 2.42) for the drugs labelled nonselective (carvedilol and labetalol, both of which also block alpha receptors).
key_findings.note: The two point estimates lie on opposite sides of 1, in the direction the unopposed-alpha hypothesis would predict, but both intervals include 1 and no test of interaction between the classes is reported; the paper describes the analysis as showing no relation for either subgroup.

key_findings.finding: Creatine kinase-MB was lower in the beta-blocker group at presentation (median 3.2 ng/ml, IQR 1.8 to 5.5, against 4.5, 2.5 to 10.5, p = 0.006) and at peak (3.2, 1.7 to 7.1, against 4.9, 2.7 to 12.2, p < 0.001), while troponin T did not differ at presentation (p = 0.12) or peak (p = 0.14).

Left ventricular ejection fraction was lower in the beta-blocker group (0.41 +/- 0.17 against 0.49 +/- 0.17, p = 0.006), and T-wave inversion was more common (56% against 26%, p < 0.001), while ST-segment depression and elevation did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, ECG changes and echocardiographic data rows

key_findings.finding: The propensity score was built from age, gender, race, character of chest pain, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, known HIV infection, previous lung disease, previous coronary artery disease, TIMI risk score, blood pressures and initial electrocardiographic findings and cardiac biomarkers, with a C statistic of 0.82; patients were stratified by propensity-score quintile and a logistic regression adjusted for quintile was fitted.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (continuing into the right column)
key_findings.note: This is stratified adjustment, not matching, although Table 3 is titled and labelled as propensity-score matching.

key_findings.finding: The authors name as limitations the retrospective design and chart-documentation quality, residual confounding beyond the variables collected, and the inability to date the cocaine use, since a urine screen can remain positive for 48 to 72 hours; they call for a prospective trial.

The authors conclude that beta-blocker use in these higher-risk patients may be safe, that the therapy was at least neutral and could potentially have been protective, and that beta-blocker treatment in cocaine-induced chest pain may be safer than previously suggested.
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' interpretation; the adjusted point estimate for the composite outcome is 1.37 with an upper confidence limit near 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The propensity-adjusted odds ratio for the composite end point is given as 1.34 in the Results text and as 1.37 in both the abstract and Table 3, with the same confidence interval (0.64 to 2.93) and p value (0.42) in each place.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two numbers is a typographical error. The difference is immaterial to the conclusion, but a claim citing this study should quote Table 3, which agrees with the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 is titled 'In-hospital outcomes before and after propensity score matching' and its column reads 'OR (95% CI) After Propensity Score Matching', while the methods and results describe stratification by propensity-score quintile with a logistic regression adjusted for that quintile, and both groups keep their full size (164 and 212) in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: No matched cohort exists. Readers who take the table at its word will overstate the balance achieved: quintile stratification leaves residual imbalance within quintiles, which matching on individuals would reduce further.

reporting_issues.issue: The myocardial infarction definition gives the local upper limit of normal for troponin T as greater than 0.1 ng/dl, while Table 2 reports troponin T in ng/ml, a thousand-fold difference in unit.
reporting_issues.consequence: The threshold that defined the main component of the composite outcome cannot be read unambiguously from the paper. The Table 2 values (medians of 0.04 with upper quartiles of 0.12 to 0.21) are consistent with ng/ml, so the methods statement appears to be the error.

reporting_issues.issue: The drug-subtype analysis is summarised as showing no independent relation for either class, although the two adjusted odds ratios lie on opposite sides of 1 (1.83 for beta-1 selective, 0.90 for carvedilol and labetalol), no interaction test is reported, and the paper does not note that both drugs in its 'nonselective' group also block alpha receptors.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one analysis in the paper that bears directly on the unopposed-alpha mechanism is reported in a way that hides it. A claim about beta blockers after cocaine should state which drugs were actually given: more than half of this treated group received an agent with alpha-blocking activity.

reporting_issues.issue: Beta-blocker exposure is defined over the first 24 hours while outcomes are counted across the whole admission, and no analysis accounts for events occurring before the drug could be given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Patients who deteriorated or died early are preferentially counted as untreated, which biases the comparison towards apparent safety of the beta blocker. The size of this effect cannot be judged from the data reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports the composite rates to one decimal (15.9% against 12.3%) while Table 3 gives whole numbers (16 against 12), and no event counts are printed anywhere in the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of events, the quantity that governs the precision of every estimate in Table 3, has to be reconstructed from percentages (about 26 per arm, editors' calculation) rather than read.
